rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “clear victory” is specifically the Ḥudaybiyah truce, not another victory.
rows.anchor: refers to the truce of Ḥudaybiyah. There is no occasion of interpreting it to refer to any other victory.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh conceded Muslim rights at the Kaʿbah after recognizing Muslim strength; expecting possible defeat (48:24), they deferred ʿumrah and offered three days in Makkah the next year.
rows.anchor: Quraysh openly accepted that Muslims too had a right on the Baytull āh.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The treaty recognized Muslims as an equal political force and accepted their right to ally with willing Arab tribes.
rows.anchor: the Quraysh accepted the Muslims as an equal political force in Arabia.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh's insistence on a ten-year no-war clause acknowledged Muslim military power.
rows.anchor: insisted to write the condition in the agreement that there shall be no war between the two for ten years.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The truce was not imposed by Muslim weakness; fighting risked harming Muslims still in Makkah, including converts who had not migrated.
rows.anchor: not because of any weakness of the Muslims; it was solely because there were many who had openly announced themselves as Muslims

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Jandal's incident and Quraysh's bigotry made Muslims feel weaker and too emotional to assess the treaty's gains and losses.
rows.anchor: In their frenzy of emotions, people could not fully reflect on the conditions of the agreement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle ل marks consequence: the clear victory is the prelude to the blessings promised to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: The particle لis to express the consequence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The victory signals that the Prophet will soon complete his mission and be relieved of its responsibilities, with his past and future sins forgiven.
rows.anchor: time is near when the Prophet will be free from the responsibilities of his mission

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second promised consequence is that God will complete His favour upon the Prophet.
rows.anchor: the Almighty will be completing his favour on him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third promised consequence is that God will open the true path of guidance for the Prophet.
rows.anchor: the Almighty will open the true way of guidance for him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth promised consequence is unassailable dominance for the Prophet.
rows.anchor: the Almighty will grant him with an unassailable dominance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrah al-Naṣr likewise joins tidings of victory and mass conversions to an indication that the Prophet's mission would be completed and he would be relieved of it.
rows.anchor: there is an indication of the fact that time would arrive when he would be relieved of his

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Sūrah al-Naṣr, the Prophet is told to glorify God, pray, and seek forgiveness as preparation for the approaching end of his mission; here the same news is explicit glad tidings suited to the context.
rows.anchor: he has been asked to prepare for it through extolling the glory of God, the prayer and asking forgiveness.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The greatest glad tidings are that the Prophet will finish his duties fully to God's satisfaction, without any liability for what was left undone.
rows.anchor: he would have befittingly discharged his obligations as a Messenger and not be held responsible

rows.speaker: Prophet (sws)
rows.claim: Asked why he worshipped strenuously despite forgiveness, the Prophet said he should be a grateful servant of his Lord.
rows.anchor: the Prophet (sws) had greatly increased the extent of his worship in his last years

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sins attributed to the Prophet are not base-desire sins: prophets never commit such sins; these are actions arising from noble motives on which God corrects them.
rows.anchor: the sins ascribed here to the Prophet (sws) do not refer to ones which are the result of following base desires; prophets of God never commit such sins

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For example, the Prophet sometimes excused hypocrites to spare them disgrace, despite recognizing their excuses as false; God corrected this graciousness because a prophet must uphold justice within divine limits.
rows.anchor: a prophet is a scale of justice in every matter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's hope that leaders' conversion would strengthen the cause was not itself sinful, but God stopped excessive attention to them when it neglected the worthy or increased the unworthy's arrogance.
rows.anchor: its worthy recipients are ignored or it causes an increase in the arrogance of the unworthy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sins meant here are the same kind of well-intentioned lapses for which the Prophet receives assurance of forgiveness.
rows.anchor: the sins attributed to the Prophet (sws) are of this nature. He was given glad tidings about all such sins that they have been forgiven.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Past and future” makes forgiveness comprehensive: it covers blemishes before and after these glad tidings without requiring another promise.
rows.anchor: the blemishes before these glad tidings have also been forgiven and those after it shall also be forgiven

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The completion of divine favour means completion of the religion, as declared at the final pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: this day [for your guidance] I have completed your religion for you and completed My favour to you

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guidance follows completion of religion: Jews and Christians lost revealed guidance, while idolaters turned Abraham and Ishmael's Kaʿbah into an idol shrine; through Muhammad, religion and the centre of monotheism were restored.
rows.anchor: This path was re-opened only after the Almighty revived and completed His religion through the Prophet Muḥammad (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The glad tidings addressed to the Prophet here are repeated for all Muslims in verse 20, where the author will explain them further.
rows.anchor: in verse 20 of this sūrah, these very glad tidings are given while addressing all the Muslims.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promised help is an unchallengeable victory over disbelief, possible only when Quraysh are humbled and Muslims become custodians of the Kaʿbah.
rows.anchor: that victory and help over disbelief which is unchallengeable and unassailable.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Ḥudaybiyah truce had weakened Quraysh's political structure, foreshadowing the conquest of Makkah; earlier Muslim successes remained challengeable while Quraysh held the city.
rows.anchor: the truce of Ḥudaybiyah had really dented their power and the time was not far when their old edifice of political power would be razed to the ground.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term for victory also carries the sense of dominance and ascendancy.
rows.anchor: besides meaning dominance and ascendancy also means

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The order of the glad tidings puts the imminent outcome last and the comprehensive, final outcome first because the Prophet's reward in the hereafter outweighed even the news of Makkah's conquest.
rows.anchor: an even greater one was to present before him the reward he would receive in the Hereafter and not much time remained when he would receive it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tranquility verse substantiates the prior promise of help: divine support miraculously gave believers courage to answer the Prophet's call to ʿumrah and strengthen their faith.
rows.anchor: It is only as a miraculous result of God’s help that the believers showed the courage to come out with the Prophet (sws) for ‘umrah at his call

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ʿumrah journey was perilous: Muslims were at war with Quraysh, who repeatedly attacked Madīnah, and 1,400–1,500 companions traveled hundreds of miles unarmed.
rows.anchor: extra ordinary for fourteen or fifteen hundred Companions (rta) to leave their homes to travel a couple of hundred miles and that too without any weapons.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hypocrites expected the journey to destroy the Muslims and believed they would not return home.
rows.anchor: the hypocrites reckoned on this very basis that the Muslims were taking themselves to destruction and this time would not be able to return home.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's gift of resolve at Ḥudaybiyah exemplified the resolve He would give believers later, ensuring the promised victory would come.
rows.anchor: just as the Almighty blessed the Prophet’s Companions with resolve at this instance, in a similar manner he will bless them with it in later phases

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Trials test believers: passing strengthens faith toward the Qur'an's contented souls, while repeated failure leads to a contrary outcome.
rows.anchor: If they succeed in these tests, their faith is strengthened
